title: Visualization of Defect Electronic States in Layered Semiconductor CrSBr
authors: Jonathan Brunette, Joost Aretz, Kiyoung Jo, Aljoscha Soll, Zdeněk Sofer, Malte Rösner, Nathan Guisinger, Adina Luican-Mayer
abstract: Chromium sulfur bromide (CrSBr) is a layered magnetic semiconducting material combining a rich magnetic phase diagram with axis-dependent electronic and optical properties. While defects in CrSBr have been shown to affect magnetic order and excitonic responses, their microscopic nature, atomic structure, and electronic properties are not yet fully understood. In this work, we use scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) to explore the structure and electronic signatures of two prominent defects in bulk CrSBr. Their structure reflects the symmetries of the underlying lattice, with electronic features near the valence band edge. By comparing experimental data with ab initio simulated STM images, we infer that a common defect corresponds to a b-axis-aligned double sulfur vacancy, in line with findings from a recent growth analysis study. This result advances our understanding of the role of intrinsic defects in shaping the electronic structure of CrSBr.
summary: This work uses STM/STS on $	ext{CrSBr}$ to investigate intrinsic defects, finding two distinct defect types. By comparing these experimental observations with DFT simulations, the authors propose that the Type 2 defect is structurally equivalent to a $b$-axis-aligned double sulfur vacancy ($	ext{V}_2	ext{S}$). This advances understanding of how native defects dictate the electronic structure and potential optical properties of layered semiconductors.
main_problem: The study aims to understand the microscopic structure, electronic properties, and nature of intrinsic defects within the layered magnetic semiconductor $	ext{CrSBr}$.
main_result: Experimental STM/STS measurements strongly suggest that a common defect corresponds to a $b$-axis-aligned double sulfur vacancy ($	ext{V}_2	ext{S}$), which is supported by qualitative agreement with DFT simulations.
method: The research combines Scanning Tunneling Microscopy/Spectroscopy (STM/STS) experiments at atomic resolution with first-principles Density Functional Theory ($	ext{DFT}+	ext{U}$) calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is $	ext{CrSBr}$, a layered magnetic semiconductor. The analysis focuses on characterizing defect states by comparing experimental electronic signatures (dI/dV maps) against theoretical predictions for various vacancy types.
key_observables: Electronic features near the valence band edge, localized electronic states centered on defects, and topographic contrast changes observed across varying bias voltages.
important_parameters: The material exhibits a bulk band gap of $1.7 \pm 0.3 	ext{ eV}$. Key defect candidates include $b$-axis-aligned double sulfur vacancies ($	ext{V}_2	ext{S}$).
main_assumptions: The comparison between simulated and experimental STM signatures is qualitative, and $	ext{DFT}+	ext{U}$ calculations are acknowledged to be approximations for weakly screened semiconductors.
figures_summary: Figures show bulk crystal structure, topographic maps identifying two defect types (Type 1 and Type 2), and comparisons of calculated band structures/simulated STM images against experimental measurements on the Type 2 defect.
paper_structure: The paper systematically uses STM to map defects, analyzes electronic signatures via STS across bias ranges, and then employs DFT calculations to model specific vacancy types ($	ext{V}_2	ext{S}$) for direct comparison with the observed defect states.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter physics, the detailed mapping of localized electronic states induced by vacancies provides a model system for studying how point defects modify band edges and potentially enable tunable emission in 2D materials, relevant to quantum emitters.
